summary: Heat stroke is a true emergency where the speed of cooling is the single biggest determinant of survival — the method of cooling matters less than getting core temperature down fast, and antipyretics have no role.
whyThisMatters: Every minute at a dangerously elevated core temperature drives ongoing cellular injury across every organ system — the difference between a good and bad outcome in heat stroke is measured in minutes of delay before effective cooling starts, which makes 'cool first, workup second' the correct instinct even though it inverts the usual diagnose-then-treat sequence.
clinicalTakeaway:
Heat stroke = hyperthermia PLUS CNS dysfunction (altered mental status, seizure, coma) in the setting of environmental/exertional heat exposure.

Cool aggressively and immediately:
- cold water immersion is fastest for a young exertional-heat-stroke patient who can tolerate it
- evaporative cooling (mist + fans) is the practical choice for an elderly or comorbid patient
- target core temperature under 39°C as fast as possible

Do NOT use antipyretics (acetaminophen/NSAIDs) — the mechanism isn't a hypothalamic-setpoint fever, so they don't work, and they can worsen a coagulopathy/hepatic injury that's often already present.

body.text:
Heat stroke = significantly elevated core temperature (classically > 40°C, though the exact number matters less than the clinical picture) PLUS CNS dysfunction — confusion, ataxia, seizure, or coma — in the setting of heat exposure/exertion.

Two classic patterns:
- EXERTIONAL heat stroke: young, healthy, often athletes/military/laborers, rapid onset, often still sweating at presentation.
- CLASSIC heat stroke: elderly, chronically ill, often on medications that impair thermoregulation (anticholinergics, diuretics, beta-blockers), slower onset over days, often anhidrotic/dry skin by the time of presentation.

Sweating status is NOT a reliable rule-out either way — don't exclude heat stroke just because the patient is still sweating.
Cooling — the single most important intervention

items: Speed matters more than method — the goal is core temperature under 39°C as fast as achievable, and the data consistently shows faster cooling correlates with better survival and less organ injury.

Cold water immersion is the fastest cooling method available and is preferred for a young, otherwise healthy, hemodynamically stable EXERTIONAL heat stroke patient who can tolerate immersion (can be logistically difficult in a hospital setting but is the standard on-scene approach at endurance events).

Evaporative cooling (undress the patient, mist/spray with lukewarm water, and use fans to maximize evaporative heat loss) is the more practical hospital approach, especially for an elderly/comorbid CLASSIC heat stroke patient where immersion may be poorly tolerated hemodynamically.
Ice packs to the neck, axillae, and groin (over major vessels) can supplement either method.

Continuous core temperature monitoring (rectal or esophageal probe — peripheral/oral/tympanic measurements are unreliable here) to track response and to STOP active cooling once target temperature is reached, avoiding overshoot into hypothermia.
Shivering during cooling increases heat production and can be counterproductive — benzodiazepines can suppress shivering if it becomes a limiting factor.

body.text: Do NOT give antipyretics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs, aspirin). Heat stroke is not a hypothalamic-setpoint fever, so antipyretics don't address the mechanism — and in a patient who may already have hepatic injury and coagulopathy from the heat stroke itself, acetaminophen and NSAIDs/aspirin add real potential harm for zero benefit.
Supportive care and complications to screen for

items: IV fluid resuscitation — but avoid over-aggressive fluid administration, since cardiac and renal injury from the heat stroke itself can limit tolerance; titrate to hemodynamics and urine output rather than a fixed volume target.
Rhabdomyolysis is common, especially in exertional heat stroke — check CK, watch for myoglobinuria, and maintain good urine output.
Coagulopathy/DIC can develop — check coags and platelets; this is part of why avoiding NSAIDs/aspirin matters.
Hepatic injury (transaminitis, and rarely acute liver failure in severe cases) and acute kidney injury are both real risks — baseline labs and trending are appropriate.
Electrolyte derangements (hyperkalemia from rhabdomyolysis, hypocalcemia, hypoglycemia) should be actively checked for and corrected.
Seizures can occur both from the heat stroke itself and from rapid electrolyte shifts during treatment — benzodiazepines are first-line if they occur.

buildNote: Kept management-focused on the cooling decision (speed and method) and the complications an ED/ICU workup needs to actively screen for, rather than an exhaustive review of thermoregulatory physiology.
